- [SRE, *Data Integrity*](https://sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity/),

All names, failure chronologies, target examples and outcomes are original teaching proposals. No runtime, WAL archive, system configuration, benchmark, restore drill or expert review was exercised in this task. The chapter is canonical in V05; its proposal-era navigation is archived.

tasks.heading: The routing contract
tasks.title: Request routing and health signals
tasks.content:
## The routing contract

A caller needs a route to an eligible instance, not a timeless list of machines. Describe
separately the externally resolved name, the service membership view, the connection
destination and the backend selected for each request. A global route may choose a location;
an internal selector chooses a process. A stale membership view can outlive a rollout.

**Gateway-routing mechanism.** A gateway matches request attributes to a declared route and
backend, then applies its policy. Routes need stable identity, precedence, versioning and an
explicit no-match behavior; the selected backend still needs its own authorization and
failure budget. Stale routes, ambiguous matches and bypass around the gateway are common.
A reverse proxy, client-side discovery or a BFF may be preferable when routing policy is
simple or the gateway would become a hidden shared dependency.

The two SRE load-balancing chapters distinguish global routing from backend selection. Their
examples support the need to examine locality, workload and selection policy; they do not
prescribe one algorithm for every service.

tasks.heading: 4. Leader elections, logs and client observations
tasks.title: Leader changes, reconfiguration and restoration
tasks.content:
## 4. Leader elections, logs and client observations

Under a Raft-style model:
1. At a time, a node believes itself a leader for a given term, but other nodes can still be unaware because messages are delayed.
2. The quorum/term/log rules govern which log entries can be committed without violating safety.
3. A newly elected leader may reconcile followers with divergent **uncommitted** suffixes.
4. An acknowledged committed log entry has a protocol-specific durability/leader-completeness guarantee, contingent on correct stable storage and membership behavior.
5. Reads require a separately defined policy: local follower reads can be stale; linearizable reads require valid confirmation/lease/read-index semantics as implemented.
6. Client retries need stable effect identity because a network error alone cannot tell whether the previous attempt committed.

A leader process's health endpoint or elected status is not the same as the cluster having
quorum and serving correct reads.

**Failure and recovery.** Elections can fail to reach quorum, split votes, or elect a
leader whose log is behind. Randomized timeouts reduce split votes; log reconciliation,
stable storage and membership rules preserve committed entries. A leader
that cannot confirm quorum must stop serving authoritative writes and linearizable reads.
Client retries still need stable effect identity because an election does not resolve an
unknown outcome. The Raft paper documents the election and log rules; the landing page recorded
here does not.

**Alternative.** Leaderless quorum coordination, static primary assignment or single-writer
partitioning may be simpler when elections add latency without a real failover
requirement. Reverse the choice when election latency and split-brain risk exceed the
coordination benefit. [Tycho causality/consensus][causality] explains order/time
relationships; [transaction/idempotency][transaction-id] explains state effects across
service boundaries.

[causality]: ../c01-time-causality-and-ordering/causality-ordering-and-consensus.md
[transaction-id]: ../../../distributed/transactional-outbox-and-idempotency.md

tasks.heading: 1. Runtime layers are not equivalent products
tasks.title: Vert.x, Netty, Quarkus, Mutiny and RxJava execution boundaries
tasks.content:
## 1. Runtime layers are not equivalent products

**Netty** is a network application framework with channels, pipelines, handlers and `EventLoopGroup` implementations. It is not itself a business workflow engine, SQL database or an automatic Reactive Streams backpressure protocol. The Netty 4.x user guide's *Writing a Discard Server* section uses separate boss/worker `NioEventLoopGroup` roles and explains how channels are assigned to event loops. This is a documented example, not a claim that every Netty deployment must use exactly two groups. [E01]

**Vert.x** provides event-driven, multi-event-loop application APIs. Its core guide describes the multi-reactor pattern, the invariant that a particular handler is not executed concurrently in its normal context, and the *Golden Rule — Don't Block the Event Loop*. `executeBlocking` moves a blocking task to workers; the guide distinguishes ordered execution for the same context and the option to allow parallel work. The worker pool is still a bounded resource. [E02]

**Quarkus** builds an application framework on Vert.x and exposes execution choices per endpoint or message handler. Quarkus 3.27 documents worker, event-loop and virtual-thread dispatch, including `@Blocking`, `@NonBlocking` and `@RunOnVirtualThread` under eligible signatures. Do not infer dispatch solely from a method's Java return type without checking the Quarkus version and extension. [E03]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    N["Netty channel + pipeline"] --> V["Vert.x event-loop dispatch"]
    V --> Q{"Quarkus endpoint / message execution"}
    Q -->|nonblocking| L["Event-loop continuation"]
    Q -->|blocking| W["Platform worker"]
    Q -->|eligible virtual| T["Virtual thread per task"]
    L --> C["Nonblocking client"]
    W --> D["Blocking client"]
    T --> D
    C --> P["Bounded downstream capacity"]
    D --> P
```

Text alternative: Netty handles channel/pipeline I/O; Vert.x dispatches event-loop work; Quarkus may run application handlers on event loops, platform workers or eligible virtual threads. All paths still reach bounded downstream capacity. This conceptual layering is not an assertion that every Quarkus extension uses every depicted path.

tasks.heading: 5. Failure modes and recovery
tasks.title: Pool failure and recovery decisions
tasks.content:
## 5. Failure modes and recovery

| Condition | What the user/operator observes | Evidence and mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Too many replicas with large independent pools | PostgreSQL connection exhaustion after scaling | Bound total replica×pool count with operating headroom |
| Pool saturated despite idle DB CPU | Waiting clients and timeouts; perhaps long-held sessions | Trace connection hold time, transaction boundaries and pool wait |
| DB already CPU/lock saturated | Larger pools worsen queue, p99 or deadlocks | Stop scaling concurrency; optimize query and admission |
| PgBouncer transaction mode breaks app | Errors or missing session state across requests | Audit driver/session features and run compatibility tests |
| Database failover | Broken/invalid connections, transaction abort, retry storm | Detect invalid connections, jitter/retry budget, idempotent commands |
| Slow connection creation after outage | Recovery lag and thundering herd | Warm pools carefully, cap simultaneous retries/connection attempts |
| Stale or leaked connection | Long-lived wait, resource exhaustion | Leak/timeout instrumentation, closing resources and lifetime limits |

### Cancellation and transaction correctness

Client cancellation can occur after a database has committed. Returning the connection to the pool or throwing a timeout does **not** prove the business operation was undone. Use logical request keys and replay/reconciliation where necessary; see [outbox and idempotency](../../../distributed/transactional-outbox-and-idempotency.md).
